threads.thread_goal: Align on current routines and main pain points before designing the new schedule.

messages.text: Kickoff for the integrated routine project for the paediatric ward and childcare unit. To move T1 forward and complete the mapping in A1, can everyone share how their current day usually runs and what tends to break down. Please include: main care tasks by time of day, cleaning and hygiene steps, meal and snack times, and any handover points that often cause confusion. I will consolidate into A1 so we can see the full picture before we start drafting the new schedule.

From early shift on the ward: 7:00–8:00 we do basic checks, help with washing and changing, and change bed linen if needed. Around 8:00–8:30 breakfast trays arrive and we help children eat and give snacks to siblings if they are allowed. Between 9:00–11:00 we support nurses with observations and treatments, plus quick toy and surface wipe downs when we can. Cleaning is not very structured; we just fit it in. Handover to late shift is around 14:30 but notes are often brief, so mood and small incidents can be missed.

On the childcare side, mornings start around 8:00 with arrivals, quick health checks, and settling activities like drawing. We usually do a group activity around 10:00, then snacks. Lunch is about 12:00. After lunch we have rest or quiet time, then free play and sometimes outdoor time. Cleaning toys and surfaces tends to happen at the end of the day if we are not too busy, so it is easy to skip when we are short staffed. I am not sure exactly how this lines up with ward medication times though.

Adding to the childcare unit view: key tasks are morning settling and emotional check in, hygiene support after toileting and before meals, structured play blocks, and end of day feedback to families. Pain points: when a child comes from the ward mid activity, we often do not know their latest treatment or rest needs, so we might offer something too stimulating. Also, we do not have a shared place to see ward routines, so coordination is mostly by quick verbal updates.

From my shifts on the ward: mornings are very packed. 7:00–9:00 is personal care, bed checks, and room tidying. 9:00–11:00 we help with procedures and observations. Around 11:30 we start preparing for lunch, making sure hands are washed and tables are clean. After lunch, 13:00–15:00, there is a mix of rest, visits, and some play. Evenings we support with snacks, hygiene, and settling for sleep. Pain points: cleaning toys and shared spaces is not clearly assigned by time or person, and handovers between us and childcare staff are informal, so tasks can fall between the cracks.

Thanks, this helps. I will log these time blocks and tasks into A1 under T1. A couple of clarifications: 1) For morning hygiene on the ward, do we consistently include toy disinfection or is it more ad hoc. 2) For handover at 14:30, what information do you usually capture about mood, pain, or behaviour, and what often gets left out.

Toy disinfection is ad hoc. We wipe toys if they look dirty or if a child has been coughing a lot, but there is no fixed time. For handover, we usually note big changes like new medication, new wounds, or if a child is very unsettled. What we miss is smaller things like a child being quieter than usual, refusing food, or small conflicts between children that might repeat later.

For the childcare unit, I can try to write down our full day with times and tasks so it is clearer for A1. I might need someone to check that I am not missing any hygiene steps that are required by the hospital rules, especially around snack and lunch times.

Happy to review your childcare unit mapping before it goes into A1. I can cross check that we include handwashing, surface cleaning, and toy rotation around meals and toileting. We should also note when we use more calming activities for children who are in pain or anxious, since that will matter for the integrated routine.

I can help check the hygiene parts against our organisational guidelines so we stay within regulations. Once you have your draft, send it and I will compare it with what we do on the ward so we can spot overlaps or gaps before we finalise A1.

From what we have so far, I see some recurring pain points: 1) Unstructured cleaning of toys and shared spaces. 2) Weak handovers between ward shifts and between ward and childcare. 3) Meal and snack times not always aligned with treatments or rest. 4) Limited visibility of each child s emotional state across areas. Are there any other major issues we should capture before we move on to designing the integrated routine.

One more pain point from the childcare side: when children come back from procedures, we often do not know if they should avoid certain activities or foods for a while. That can lead to offering something that clashes with their care plan. So lack of clear guidance after procedures should be on the list.

Agree with that list. I would add that we sometimes double up on tasks, like both ward and childcare staff trying to organise the same play activity or both assuming the other cleaned a shared playroom. That wastes time and still leaves some things undone.

For me the hardest moments are when meal times shift because of treatments. I am never sure if I should wait, give a snack, or push ahead with the planned time. Maybe we can have clearer guidance in the new routine for those situations.

I think the main issues are covered now. For the next step, it might help to agree on which daily tasks are non negotiable so they must appear in the integrated routine, and which ones are more flexible. That will guide T2 later.

Proposed list of core daily tasks that must be in the integrated routine: 1) Personal hygiene and basic care (washing, changing, toileting support). 2) Medication and treatment support in line with nursing plans. 3) Structured cleaning and disinfection of rooms, toys, and shared surfaces. 4) Meal and snack distribution with hand hygiene before and after. 5) Rest and quiet time blocks. 6) Emotional check ins and basic play or comfort activities. 7) Shift handovers including mood, incidents, and hygiene status. If no one objects, I will record this as our core task list for D1 and use it as the base for T2.

That list works for me. For the first version, I suggest we prioritise fixing: 1) structured cleaning and disinfection, 2) clearer handovers, and 3) alignment of meals with treatments and rest. Emotional support is already happening but could be better documented, so maybe that is just behind the top three.

I agree with those priorities for D2. If we get cleaning, handovers, and meal timing right in the first version, it should already reduce infection risk and confusion a lot. We can then refine emotional support activities in more detail when we work on the activity plan.

threads.thread_goal: Review and finalise the draft integrated routine and hygiene checklist.

messages.text: I have posted the first draft of the integrated daily routine and the hygiene checklist in A3 and A2, based on what we mapped in A1 and the scope of T2, T3, and T5. The routine covers morning, midday, afternoon, and evening blocks for both ward and childcare unit, and the checklist lists cleaning tasks with frequencies and responsible roles. Please review and comment on timings, overlaps, and anything that looks unrealistic for your shift.

Thanks for pulling this together. Looking at A3, the morning block 7:00–9:00 includes personal care, basic observations, and first toy wipe down at 8:45. On the ward that might clash with breakfast support, which is usually 8:00–8:30 and often runs late. I suggest moving the first toy and surface disinfection to 9:15, after breakfast trays are cleared, so we are not trying to clean while children are still eating.

On the late shift, A3 shows a 17:00–17:30 snack and then 17:30–18:00 cleaning of play areas. That seems fine, but we often have treatments around 17:00. Maybe we should note in the routine that if a child has a procedure in that window, we either bring the snack earlier or later, and record it in the handover so the next shift knows. Not sure how to phrase that in the schedule though.

I looked at the hygiene checklist in A2. It says toys in shared playroom disinfected three times a day. I am worried that I will forget the midday one when the unit is busy. Could we maybe link those times to fixed routine points, like after morning snack, after lunch, and before closing, so it is easier to remember.

Linking toy disinfection to snack and lunch times makes sense. In childcare we can do: after morning snack, after lunch, and at the end of the day. That way it is tied to existing tasks. For the ward, maybe after breakfast, after afternoon snack, and before night settling. We should reflect that in A2 so it is clear for everyone.

Good point on breakfast. I will adjust A3 so the first ward toy and surface disinfection is at 9:15 instead of 8:45. For the late shift snack and treatments, we can add a note in the routine that snack time can move by up to 30 minutes around procedures, and that any change must be written in the handover notes. That keeps it flexible but still documented.

Agree with that approach. To avoid conflicts with medication, we should also check A3 against the usual medication rounds with the nursing team before we finalise D3. I can take a pass with one of the nurses to confirm that our time blocks do not clash with standard treatment windows.

On the hygiene checklist A2, there is a line for cleaning high touch surfaces every two hours on the ward. That is ideal, but on very busy days it might not be realistic. Could we define a minimum, like every four hours, with an extra clean after visible contamination or high traffic, so we do not set ourselves up to fail.

That is a fair concern. For the pilot, we can set high touch surfaces to every four hours as the standard, plus after visible contamination, and see if we can manage more often in practice. I will update A2 accordingly and flag it to the infection control specialist for feedback as part of T3.

For meals in A3, the childcare unit lunch is set at 12:00–12:30 and ward lunch at 12:30–13:00. That might make it hard to coordinate if siblings are in both places. Would it be better to overlap them more, or is the staggered timing intentional to reduce pressure on dietary services.

The staggered timing was to avoid overloading dietary services, but you are right about siblings. Maybe we can keep the main delivery times as they are for now and add a note in T5 that siblings can have a flexible window between 12:00–13:00, coordinated with the dietary supervisor. I will check feasibility with them before we lock D3.

From the childcare perspective, the time blocks in A3 look workable: morning structured activity 9:30–10:30, outdoor or movement 14:00–15:00, and calm play 16:00–17:00. As long as we keep the hygiene steps from A2 tied to snack and lunch, I am comfortable with this layout for the pilot.

Summarising proposed adjustments before we close D3 and D4: 1) Move first ward toy and surface disinfection to 9:15. 2) Allow snack time to shift by up to 30 minutes around procedures, with changes recorded in handover. 3) Link toy disinfection in A2 to snack and lunch times and end of day. 4) Set high touch surface cleaning to every four hours plus after visible contamination. 5) Keep staggered lunches but allow a flexible window for siblings, pending confirmation from dietary services under T5. If there are no further objections, I suggest we approve these time blocks and the updated checklist for the pilot.

I am aligned with that summary. Once we get the quick check from infection control on A2 and from dietary services on the sibling lunch window in T5, I think we can treat D3 and D4 as confirmed for the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Align on the activity plan and how to support children emotionally during the new routine.

messages.text: I have drafted a weekly activity plan in A4, aligned with the time blocks in A3 and the scope of T4. It includes at least two structured activities per day, with options for different ages and energy levels. Please review and share if the activities feel realistic during your shifts, and how we can best support children who are in pain, anxious, or recovering from procedures.

Looking at A4, I like the morning group story time and the afternoon movement games. My concern is that on some days we are short on staff, and running a full group activity might be hard. Maybe we should mark some activities as optional or as small group versions so we do not feel we are failing if we cannot do the full plan.

From the ward side, the calm activities in A4, like drawing and quiet games, fit well with rest times in A3. The more active ones, like mini obstacle courses, might clash with children who just had procedures. Maybe we can have a calm alternative listed for each active activity so we can switch easily.

I like that A4 includes emotional check in moments at the start of morning and afternoon blocks. On the ward, we can use simple questions or visual scales to see how children feel. It would help if the plan also suggests how to record key mood changes so they can be picked up in handovers and in the pilot feedback for T9.

We can link those emotional check ins to the handover template in A6. For example, we could add a simple mood scale and a short note field in T7 so that if a child is very anxious or withdrawn, it is clearly visible for the next shift and for the childcare unit.

Good point on staffing. For the pilot, I suggest we treat some activities as mandatory anchors and others as optional. For example, daily morning emotional check in and at least one calm structured activity should be mandatory, while larger group games and special themed sessions can be optional depending on capacity.

I like that split. If we say morning emotional check in and one calm activity are must do, I feel more confident. On busy days we can still offer small things like drawing or puzzles without trying to run big group games.

Agree. On the ward, I would also make bedtime calming routines mandatory, like reading or soft music, because they help with sleep and reduce anxiety. More energetic activities should stay optional and only for children cleared by nurses.

To keep it simple for D5, maybe we define mandatory activities as: 1) morning emotional check in, 2) one calm structured activity in the morning or early afternoon, 3) bedtime calming routine for children staying overnight. Optional: group movement games, themed sessions, and extra crafts. We can still log all of them in T9 feedback to see what children and families value most.

That matches what I had in mind. I will update A4 to clearly label those three as mandatory for the pilot and mark the rest as optional. During T9, I will collect feedback from children and families on both mandatory and optional activities so we can refine after the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Prepare for the pilot week, including handover process and logging of incidents.

messages.text: Pilot announcement: we plan to start the one week pilot of the integrated routine next Monday, using the schedule in A3, hygiene checklist in A2, and handover template in A6, linked to T7 and T8. Before we begin, we need to agree how and when to use the handover notes each shift and what we count as an incident to log in A7. Please share how this would work best in your shifts.

For the handover template in A6, I suggest we use it at three fixed points: end of early shift, end of late shift, and when a child moves between ward and childcare. The shift handovers would cover hygiene status, meals, mood, and incidents, while the transfer notes would focus on current restrictions, recent procedures, and emotional state.

Using A6 at every child transfer might be heavy if we are very busy. Could we have a short version for transfers, maybe just key boxes for recent medication, activity restrictions, and mood, and keep the full template for shift changes.

From the childcare side, I support fixed times for full handovers at shift end, plus a very short transfer note when a child arrives from the ward. If we keep it to a few tick boxes and one line of text, it should be manageable. We can test this during the first two days of the pilot and adjust if it is too heavy.

I am a bit worried about remembering to fill A6 every time. Could we add a small reminder in A3, like a note at the end of each shift block saying complete handover notes, so it is part of the routine and not an extra thing we might forget.

Good idea. For D6, I propose: 1) Full A6 handover notes completed at the end of each shift for all children. 2) A short transfer section within A6 used when a child moves between ward and childcare, limited to key restrictions, recent procedures, and mood. 3) Reminders added to A3 at the end of each shift block. We will test this during the pilot and adjust if it proves too heavy.
I am comfortable with that for D6. I will update A6 and T7 to include a short transfer section and add the shift end reminders into A3 before Monday.

Next, we need to define what counts as an incident for A7 during T8. My suggestion: 1) Any deviation from the routine that affects safety, hygiene, or medication timing. 2) Any fall, injury, or near miss. 3) Significant behavioural or emotional events, like prolonged distress or aggression. 4) Missed or delayed meals that could impact wellbeing. What do you think.
I agree with that list. Maybe we should also log if hygiene steps in A2 are skipped or delayed, for example if a toy disinfection round is missed, so we can see how realistic the checklist is.

From the childcare side, I would add any strong feedback from families about the new routine, positive or negative, as an incident type for A7. It will help when we later summarise feedback in T9 and adjust in T10.

I am not always sure what counts as a near miss. Could we give a couple of examples in A7, like a child almost falling from a chair but being caught, or a meal almost given to the wrong child but corrected in time.

Yes, we can add examples to A7. For near misses, we can list: almost giving the wrong meal, almost missing a hygiene step that is caught in time, or a child nearly injuring themselves but being stopped. That should make it clearer for everyone.

To close D7, here is the agreed list for the pilot: incidents to log in A7 during T8 are 1) any deviation from A3 that affects safety, hygiene, or medication timing, 2) any fall, injury, or near miss, 3) significant behavioural or emotional events, 4) missed or delayed meals that could impact wellbeing, 5) skipped or delayed hygiene steps from A2, and 6) strong feedback from families about the new routine. We will include short examples in A7 so everyone has the same understanding.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and decide on adjustments before wider rollout.

messages.text: Pilot week is complete. I have summarised observations and incidents in A7 under T8, and linked them to the routine in A3, hygiene checklist in A2, activity plan in A4, and orientation guide draft in A5. Key themes: some hygiene steps were hard to keep on time, handover notes in A6 improved communication but took longer than expected, and families gave mixed feedback on meal timing and activities. Let us review and decide what to keep, modify, or drop for the final routine for D8.

From the ward perspective, the new time blocks in A3 mostly worked. The main issue was high touch surface cleaning every four hours; on two days we logged missed rounds in A7. It might be better to tie those cleans more tightly to natural breaks, like after breakfast, after lunch, and after afternoon snack, instead of strict clock times.

In childcare, the toy disinfection linked to snack and lunch in A2 was easier to remember, but I still missed the end of day round once, which is in A7. Maybe we can add a visual reminder near the exit or in the orientation guide A5 so it is more visible at closing time.

Feedback from children and families collected for T9: they liked the predictable morning emotional check in and bedtime calming routines from A4. Some found the afternoon movement block too tiring on days with many procedures. Families appreciated clearer explanations of the routine, but a few said the orientation felt long. We might need to simplify A5 and keep the most important points up front.

On handovers, A6 clearly improved information flow, especially around mood and incidents. However, several entries in A7 mention that completing the full template at each shift end took longer than planned. Maybe we can shorten some sections or use more tick boxes so it is faster while keeping the key content.

Looking at A7 and the T9 summary, I suggest we keep as is: 1) morning emotional check in, 2) one calm structured activity per day, and 3) bedtime calming routines. We should modify: 1) afternoon movement activities to be shorter and clearly optional for children who had procedures, and 2) the orientation guide A5 to be more concise, with a one page quick start and details later.

I agree with tying high touch cleaning to natural breaks. If we set it to after each main meal or snack in A3, it will be easier to remember and still frequent enough. We can keep the rule of extra cleaning after visible contamination from A2.
A simple poster with the end of day hygiene steps from A2 near the door would help me a lot. If we add that idea into A5, new staff will also see it from day one.

I can adjust A4 so that afternoon movement is clearly marked as optional and includes calm alternatives for children who are tired or in pain. I will also highlight in T9 follow up that families appreciated the calm options, so we keep those central in the final plan.

For A6, I propose we keep the sections on hygiene, meals, mood, and incidents, but reduce free text fields and add more tick boxes. That should cut down writing time. We can also add a short reminder in A5 that handovers should be concise and focused on changes since last shift.

On meal timing, A7 shows a few incidents where snacks were delayed due to procedures, but the flexible window we defined in T5 seemed to work when used. I suggest we keep the flexible window and make it more visible in A3 and A5, so staff feel confident using it without worrying they are breaking the routine.
Yes, when we used the flexible window it reduced stress for both staff and children. Making it clearer in A3 and A5 should help everyone use it consistently.

For the orientation guide A5, I can draft a one page quick start that covers: key time blocks from A3, hygiene expectations from A2, main activities from A4, and how to use A6. The rest of the guide can stay as reference for those who want more detail.

To prepare for wider rollout under T10, we should list our final adjustments: 1) tie high touch cleaning to meal and snack breaks, 2) add visual reminders for end of day hygiene, 3) simplify A6 with more tick boxes, 4) mark afternoon movement as optional with calm alternatives in A4, 5) shorten A5 with a quick start page, and 6) make the flexible meal window more visible in A3 and A5. If everyone agrees, we can record this as D8.

I agree with that list for D8. Once we apply these changes in A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6 under T10, we can share the updated package with the head nurse, ward manager, childcare coordinator, infection control, and dietary services for confirmation before wider rollout.
